audio_caption: The audio clip begins with a male speaker who is asking questions about "drug reform" and what his guest thinks about leaving the issue "to the people." A second male speaker responds, indicating that he doesn't think people should go to "jail for smoking a joint" and he would be in favor of decriminalization. He states his position is from a health perspective rather than a crime perspective. The first speaker highlights the shift in the debate towards health issues and asks if it should be treated like alcohol. The second speaker acknowledges this and mentions a health study regarding the impact of marijuana smoking on bipolar problems. He stresses the need to consider the implications if they were to go down the path of decriminalization. The first speaker then changes the topic to "law and order." The clip is recorded in a reasonably quiet environment, with some background sounds that don't interfere with the dialogue.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker inquiring about the government's handling of law and order. The second male speaker replies in a critical tone, citing "three strikes" as an example of measures originating "out of the south," then discusses prison population statistics, noting that "50% of our prison population is functionally illiterate." He notes, "80% of them came in on alcohol and drug issues," and claims that substance abuse rehabilitation is beneficial. He then notes that some criminals, maybe "10, maybe 20%," are "hardcore," adding that these should be incarcerated.

The audio features two male speakers discussing imprisonment rates and recidivism. The first speaker proposes a topic for discussion in a neutral tone. The second speaker responds, emphasizing that he finds the current statistics "appalling" and "astronomically high." His tone is serious, conveying concern about the issue. He mentions percentages related to recidivism rates.

The audio clip begins with two male speakers engaged in a somewhat heated debate, disagreeing on who is responsible for certain policies, with phrases like "national party" and "labor government" being mentioned. The tone is argumentative but also contains moments of nervous laughter. One of the speakers suggests, with a more measured tone, that there is a "turning around" regarding sentencing sentiment. He further explains that people believe $90,000 spent to keep somebody in jail is a "complete waste of money". He says locking people away longer so recidivism rates are higher when they come out is a “dumb thing to do”.

The clip begins with a man questioning whether Labor and National parties are "just following the crowd" and indicating that they don't seem to be at the forefront of the debate. Another man responds, stating there's definitely an issue around short-term prevention and long-term issues. He explains that media attention focuses on the number of police on the street, which he acknowledges as important, but some other issues are longer-term. Finally, someone announces they have a question from the floor.

The audio features speech from two individuals, one sounding like a reporter, the other presumably a politician. The reporter asks about education policies, specifically regarding universal student allowances, quoting the politician's policy as vague. The politician confirms the policy has been their goal since the beginning. This dialogue takes place amidst noticeable background noise.

The audio clip features a single male speaker discussing the possibility of a universal student allowance. Initially, he expresses the desirability of such a program but then states, with a slightly serious tone, that "we're just not going to be close to being able to do that, we just simply can't afford it." His tone then shifts as he mentions efforts to address the issue, noting "cap on...fees...keeping the interest obviously off," and hoping to become "a bit more flexible."

The clip starts with a male speaker discussing tertiary policy, describing it as a combination of three things: access to university regardless of circumstances, maintaining the quality of universities, and preventing the best brains from leaving New Zealand. He speaks in a conversational tone. A second male speaker responds, wondering if this approach is part of the problem with the Labour party, in that they can't differentiate themselves enough from the National party. The first speaker begins to respond.

The audio clip begins with two male speakers engaged in a conversation. One speaker, using a natural and conversational tone, claims that he had to fight his economics team regarding tertiary policy. He continues by saying he had to compromise to ensure that students were not disadvantaged. He then said that he also wanted to make sure that universities at least kept pace with inflation and look at the post-doc scholarships. The other speaker said he sees time is almost up and prompts him to make final election predictions.

The audio clip features a male speaker discussing the performance of the Greens, suggesting they are doing well and could possibly improve from last time. His tone is conversational and analytical. He also mentions that they come down off a "high," and notes that they "could be". There is some ambient background noise with an indiscernible quality.

The clip begins with a male speaker questioning if someone is a "one-trick, one MP pony." Another male voice responds, speaking about struggling to get MPs, then mentions a politician by name, hoping he gets to a specific location. He clarifies that he is friends with this person and thinks they would be a good MP. He notes that this politician is behind in a small poll but has a good chance. The first male speaker then asks if something "could be wiped out." The second male speaker responds, saying "could be," followed by "they're done."

The audio clip begins with a male voice asking about Act and what is going to happen to them. In a conversational tone, another male voice explains that Ipswich voters this time are saying "enough", citing a small group of voters he was at a table with the other night.  He notes these "so-called blue voters", who have said they do not want to vote for banks. He adds that people have forgotten that Hyde was a very good constituent MP. The first male voice asks about Winston Peters, assessing his chances of being back. The second male answers that he thinks it's probably 35 percent, and concludes that he wouldn't rule this guy out.

The audio begins with a speaker inquiring if the National party is likely to receive a high percentage of votes. A male speaker responds, hoping not, saying that a party hasn't received more than 50% of votes since 1951, so it's not possible.
He adds that people are looking at what's happening with parties rather than political blocks. The speaker continues, asking about the majority, at 10,000 votes. A male speaker states no, it was in a by-election. He then mentions he would be happy to maintain or improve his majority, because he has worked incredibly hard.
After some unclear dialogue, the male speaker says he would like to think that he could stay the same or better. He thanks the person, who responds with an "appreciate," followed by applause.
